transcript:
Meeting header:
Date: 2026-10-21
Start time: 15:00 PDT
Duration: ~52 minutes
Attendees: Alex Kim (Redwood AE), Priya Bhatia (Redwood SE), Jordan Lee (Redwood SE); Marcus Lee (Civitas Head of ML), Dana Ortiz (Eng Manager), Priya Sharma (Security), Evan Park (Data Eng)

Auto-summary (auto-gen, may be rough):
- Goal: scope a 3-week POC to validate latency, cost, and structured output/ tool-calling integrations for Civitas' insights product.
- Success criteria: 95th percentile latency < 300ms for short infer calls; throughput support for 120 qps burst to 300 qps with batching; structured JSON output accuracy >= 92% on extraction tasks; security controls validated (SAML + KMS).
- Next steps: SOW, benchmark run, security questionnaire, sizing artifacts.

Transcript:
[00:00] Alex Kim: Hey everyone, thanks for joining. Uh, I'll kick us off - Alex from Redwood, AE. Priya and Jordan from the SE team with me. Marcus, Dana, Evan - thanks for taking the time.
[00:12] Marcus Lee: Hi all, thanks. Quick note - we're running late on a release so hopefully we can keep to 45-ish? But yeah, main objective is to scope the POC: success criteria, workloads, and integration approach.
[00:25] Priya Bhatia: Perfect. I've got an agenda: confirm success criteria, go through workload sizing, discuss benchmarks and timelines, and then integration options - SDKs, openai-compatible endpoints, function/tool calling and structured outputs.
[00:38] Dana Ortiz: Sounds good. For context, our product is realtime insight extraction from meeting transcripts and support tickets. Typical request sizes are 200-600 tokens, with a subset of short prompts ~40-80 tokens. We'll likely run both batch offline jobs and near-real-time endpoints.
[00:55] Evan Park: To add - current traffic baseline is about 40 qps steady with spikes to ~180 qps during morning syncs. Average payload size is 3KB. We can share logs.
[01:10] Priya Bhatia: Great, that helps. For the POC we usually size for expected production plus buffer. If you're seeing 180 qps spikes, we often test 2x (so 360 qps) for burst durability. Do you have latency SLOs?
[01:23] Marcus Lee: Our product target is sub-300ms p95 for the short prompt path. For longer extraction jobs p95 can be up to 1s, but we want predictability. Cost target is important too - we need to compare hosted vs dedicated for unit cost.
[01:38] Jordan Lee: Understood. Typical Redwood approach: we run a 3-day benchmark using your sample payloads and our benchmark harness. We'll test OpenAI-compatible endpoint (same prompt/response shape), and also test our SDK integration to evaluate streaming, function/tool-calling features and structured JSON return.
[01:52] Dana Ortiz: When you say OpenAI-compatible endpoint, do you mean the API will accept the exact same POST body? We're using an internal abstraction that expects that.
[01:59] Priya Bhatia: Yes, our OpenAI-compatible endpoints take the same basic JSON - messages or prompt, max_tokens, temperature - and we also support function_call / tool calling patterns with the same fields. There are small vendor-specific params but we keep the surface consistent so minimal code changes.
[02:14] Marcus Lee: Nice. That's a big win. We rely heavily on function calling for structured extraction - we call a parse function with a JSON schema and expect a typed response. How mature is your function-calling?
[02:24] Priya Bhatia: We've got a couple of flavours. The OpenAI-compatible function_call works for many cases; we also have a more explicit structured-output helper in the SDK that can validate and coerce responses to the schema. It's not magic - it's regex/LM-assisted postprocessing plus fallback heuristics. We'll demo during the POC.
[02:41] Marcus Lee: Okay - accuracy of structured extraction is our primary quality metric. We need at least 92% field-level accuracy on our eval set.
[02:50] Alex Kim: We'll add that to the success criteria. For benchmarks we typically run: latency (p50/p95/p99), throughput with gradual ramp, and a correctness pass for structured output against your labeled dataset. Also cost projection.
[03:03] Evan Park: On data: can Redwood run benchmarks in our VPC or does it need to be in Redwood hosted? We have data residency requirements for some datasets.
[03:12] Priya Sharma: Right - security questions. We need to validate SAML SSO, audit logs, KMS key usage and retention. SOC2 scope is already on their site but need more detail.
[03:21] Priya Bhatia: For POC we can do two modes: 1) run hosted benchmarks against a synthetic sample (no real data), or 2) run in your VPC/private deployment for full security posture tests. Private runs take more lead time; typically 2-3 weeks to stand up in a customer's VPC depending on networking.
[03:38] Dana Ortiz: Time is a constraint. Which path is faster to get meaningful numbers?
[03:42] Jordan Lee: Hosted benchmark is fastest - we can run the harness within 48 hours after we get sample payloads and the SOW signed. VPC deployment gives more accurate latency (since it's closer to your infra) and certs. But if you need security review early, we can do hosted synthetic first, then migrate to VPC for the final validation.
[03:58] Marcus Lee: That sounds reasonable. We'll do a hosted run to start. Can you confirm what telemetry you need from us for sizing?
[04:05] Priya Bhatia: Ideally: per-request token counts, qps distributions (1m/5m/60m), peak qps, percent of short vs long prompts, and typical concurrency per user. Logs and a small representative eval set for accuracy tests. Evan, you mentioned you can share logs?
[04:20] Evan Park: Yes - I'll extract a week of anonymized logs and sample payloads. I'll scrub PII and send a secure link.
[04:27] Alex Kim: Excellent. On the POC timeline - proposed: Week 1 (prep): share SOW, sample data, and benchmark harness; Week 2: run 3-day benchmark (we do multiple runs); Week 3: analysis, run follow-ups for edge cases, security review and final results + recommendation. So a 3-week cycle.
[04:45] Dana Ortiz: That maps well with our quarter planning. One question about SDKs: our stack is TypeScript backend + Go workers. Do you have official SDKs for both?
[04:55] Priya Bhatia: We have first-class JS/TS SDK with streaming, function-calling and structured-output helpers. Go SDK is supported but a bit lower feature-parity - it supports standard request/response and streaming, but some of the structured helpers are in JS only. If needed, we can provide a small wrapper or examples in Go.
[05:12] Marcus Lee: Do you support embeddings and reranking as part of the POC? We do hybrid retrieval-augmented generation and want to test embeddings quality and cost.
[05:20] Jordan Lee: Yes - embeddings endpoints are in scope. We'll include a reranking workload in the benchmark so you can see cost/throughput tradeoffs. We'll also show quantization and batching recommendations to lower unit costs.
[05:31] Marcus Lee: Great. On the dedicated vs hosted discussion - would the POC help us compare unit costs?
[05:36] Alex Kim: Absolutely. The benchmark harness produces a baseline per-token and per-query cost estimate for hosted and for a dedicated pool with the same model config. For dedicated we factor in reserved capacity amortization. We'll provide those numbers in the final report.
[05:48] Priya Sharma: For security: we need to know whether logs include user-level identifiers, how long logs are retained, and whether keys can be customer-managed (KMS/HSM). Also, regulatory requirement: we need an audit log that shows who accessed what data.
[06:02] Priya Bhatia: For hosted POC we can configure log redaction and shorter retention. Customer-managed KMS is available in Dedicated/Private. Audit logs are available and can be exported to your SIEM. We'll send the security architecture doc and the SOC2/ISO scopes.
[06:15] Dana Ortiz: Any gotchas with function calling mapping to our existing schema? We use nested objects and arrays.
[06:22] Jordan Lee: The SDK's structured-output postprocessing handles nested schemas but there are edge cases - for example, deeply nested arrays sometimes need a few prompt-engineering tweaks. We'll test your real examples during the POC. If needed we can add a small deterministic parser step.
[06:36] Marcus Lee: On model variants - we use an open model family for cost reasons. Do you support multiple quantized variants?
[06:43] Priya Bhatia: Yes, we can serve multiple model variants and recommend quantization profiles per workload. The benchmark will include a quality vs latency vs cost matrix so you can pick the right tradeoff.
[06:54] Evan Park: For the benchmark harness - what's the interface, and can we run it ourselves?
[06:58] Priya Bhatia: We'll provide a GitHub repo with the harness (scripted replay of requests, metrics exporter to Prometheus), and instructions to run either against our hosted endpoint or your VPC. We'll also share a Google Sheet with the results template.
[07:10] Marcus Lee: Excellent. A few clarifying items for the success criteria recap?
[07:15] Alex Kim: Sure - I'll read back what I have: 1) Latency: p95 < 300ms for short prompts, p95 < 1s for long prompts; 2) Throughput: handle steady 40 qps and tolerate bursts up to 360 qps with graceful queuing; 3) Structured extraction accuracy >= 92% on your labeled eval set; 4) Security: SAML SSO, KMS support (or an equivalent in Hosted with redaction), and audit logs validated; 5) Cost projection: hosted vs dedicated delta and recommendation. Anything to add?
[07:38] Marcus Lee: Add embeddings quality threshold and reranking correctness - maybe an nDCG target? But for now let's say embeddings/semantic search quality must be comparable to our current baseline (we'll provide metrics).
[07:48] Dana Ortiz: Also add SDK parity test for JS & Go - we need working examples.
[07:52] Alex Kim: Noted. We'll include SDK integration as a pass/fail item.
[07:55] Priya Sharma: One more: logging retention and deletion proof for PII - need to be discussed with legal.
[08:02] Alex Kim: We'll include a legal/security call after the benchmarks.
[08:05] Marcus Lee: Timeline question - if we sign the SOW Monday (2026-10-25), can you start benchmarks that week?
[08:12] Alex Kim: If you sign by Monday and provide sample payloads and the eval set, we can usually kick off the hosted benchmark Wednesday and run through Friday. We'll aim for the week of Oct 26 for runs.
[08:22] Dana Ortiz: OK. A few small implementation questions - streaming vs non-streaming: our realtime path prefers streaming to reduce perceived latency. How's streaming support?
[08:30] Jordan Lee: Full streaming support in the JS SDK; streaming in other SDKs exists but may need custom code. For streaming we also support prefix caching on the runtime (KV cache) to keep token costs down; that helps in conversational state.
[08:43] Evan Park: You mentioned KV cache - can you clarify? I think our team called it 'K V cache' in docs and sometimes it's transcribed oddly.
[08:48] Priya Bhatia: Yeah, it's the token key-value cache maintained by the runtime to avoid recomputation for long context windows. We'll share a short doc on cache semantics and how it impacts latency.
[08:58] Marcus Lee: Great. Anything else on integration shape?
[09:01] Alex Kim: We'll send a short integration checklist: 1) API keys & access, 2) SDK examples (TS + Go), 3) benchmark harness + dataset, 4) SOW. Expect that in email within 48 hours.
[09:12] Priya Sharma: And please include the security doc and SOC2 attachments.
[09:15] Alex Kim: Will do.
[09:17] Dana Ortiz: Perfect. Last logistic - who's the main technical contact on the Civitas side for the bench runs?
[09:22] Evan Park: That'll be me. I'll coordinate with Marcus and Dana.
[09:26] Alex Kim: Excellent. We'll follow up with the SOW and link to the harness. Thanks everyone.
[09:30] Marcus Lee: Thanks, appreciate it.
